title: Assyria
lead: The empire on the upper Tigris, ruled from Asshur, Calah (Nimrud), Dur-Sharrukin and Nineveh, that dominated the Near East from the ninth to the late seventh century BC. It destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel (722 BC), made Judah a vassal, and fell to the Babylonians and Medes (612–609 BC).

sections.b: Asshur appears in Genesis among the descendants of Shem and as the land Nimrod built Nineveh in (Genesis 10:11, 22). Assyria enters Israel's history with Shalmaneser III, who fought Ahab at Qarqar (853 BC) and took tribute from Jehu (841), though the Bible mentions neither event. In 2 Kings it comes onstage with "Pul" (Tiglath-pileser III), who takes Menahem's silver (2 Kings 15:19–20), carves away Galilee and Gilead (2 Kings 15:29) and answers Ahaz's plea by taking Damascus (2 Kings 16:7–9). Shalmaneser V besieges Samaria, which falls in 722 (2 Kings 17:3–6); Sargon II, who completed Samaria's conquest, is named in the Bible only once, when his commander takes Ashdod (Isaiah 20:1). Sennacherib invades Judah in 701 (2 Kings 18:13–19:37). The prophets call Assyria the rod of God's anger that will itself be broken (Isaiah 10:5–19), Jonah preaches to Nineveh, and Nahum celebrates its fall.
